summary: A republication of PKCS #10 version 1.7 from RSA Laboratories, defining a syntax for certification requests. Change control remains within the PKCS process.

plainLanguage.summary: When you want an official ID card for your digital key, you fill out a form. This defines the form.

subtitle: The standard form for asking a certificate authority to turn your public key into a certificate.

tldr.problem: An entity that has a key pair needs a standard way to ask a certification authority for an X.509 certificate that binds its name to its public key.
tldr.mechanism: A certification request holds the subject's distinguished name, its public key and optional attributes, signed with the subject's private key, and is written in ASN.1 and DER encoded before signing.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2986 republishes PKCS #10 version 1.7 from RSA Laboratories, with change control left in the PKCS process. It obsoletes RFC 2314 and is updated by RFC 5967.

today: RFC 2986 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 2314 and is updated by RFC 5967. The RFC says change control stays with the PKCS process.

sections.title: What a Certification Request Is
sections.content:
A certification request consists of a distinguished name, a public key, and optionally a set of attributes, all signed by the entity asking for certification. It is sent to a certification authority, which turns it into an X.509 public-key certificate.

How the authority returns the certificate is outside the scope of the document, and a PKCS #7 message is named as one possibility. The attributes serve two purposes: giving other information about the entity, such as a challenge password it may later use to request revocation, and supplying attributes for inclusion in X.509 certificates. Authorities may also require non-electronic forms.

The RFC states that it is a republication of PKCS #10 v1.7, that change control stays with the PKCS process, and that its body, apart from the security considerations section, is taken directly from the PKCS documents.
sections.plainLanguage: You write down your name and your secret-lock's matching public key, sign the page, and hand it to the office that issues ID cards.

sections.title: How a Request Is Built and Used
sections.content:
A request has three parts: the certification request information, a signature algorithm identifier, and a digital signature over the information. The requester first builds a CertificationRequestInfo value, signs it with the subject's private key, then collects the information, the algorithm identifier and the signature into a CertificationRequest.

The certification authority fulfills the request by authenticating the requester and verifying its signature. If the request is valid, it builds an X.509 certificate from the name and public key, its own issuer name, and its own choice of serial number, validity period and signature algorithm. It may also use PKCS #9 attributes in the request to build certificate extensions.

The RFC adds four notes. An entity would typically send a request after generating a key pair. The signature stops an entity from requesting a certificate for another party's public key. How the request reaches the authority is out of scope, and paper is possible. The syntax is not compatible with the one in RFC 1424, and is designed to minimize request size, which matters for authorities accepting paper requests.
sections.plainLanguage: The office checks that you really are who you say, checks your signature proves you hold the secret key, and then prints the card with its own serial number and expiry date.

sections.title: The Request Syntax
sections.content:
The syntax is written in ASN.1. CertificationRequestInfo is a SEQUENCE of four parts: version, subject, subjectPKInfo and attributes. The version is 0 for this version of the standard. The subject is the distinguished name of the entity whose key is to be certified. The public key info names the key algorithm, with rsaEncryption from PKCS #1 as an example, and carries the key as a bit string. The attributes are a set of extra information, such as the PKCS #9 challenge-password or the extensionRequest attribute.

CertificationRequest is a SEQUENCE of the certificationRequestInfo, a signatureAlgorithm and a signature bit string. Specific algorithm and attribute objects are left to specifications that reference this document, using extension markers so that additions stay interoperable with future versions.
sections.plainLanguage: The form has fixed boxes in a fixed order: a version number, your name, your public key, extra details, and at the bottom the way you signed it and the signature.

sections.title: Signing the Request
sections.content:
Signing takes two steps. First the certificationRequestInfo value is DER encoded, giving an octet string. Second, that octet string is signed with the subject's private key under the chosen signature algorithm, giving the bit string stored in signature.

For the signature algorithm, the RFC gives md5WithRSAEncryption from PKCS #1 as an example of an object a specification might add to the allowed signature algorithms. It also shows an equivalent way to write the type using a generic SIGNED wrapper.
sections.plainLanguage: You press your personal stamp over the finished form. Anyone can later check the stamp matches your public key, so nobody else could have made it.

sections.title: Version 1.7 and Security
sections.content:
Version 1.7 refers to X.680 through X.690, the then-current ASN.1 standards, and drops all references to X.208 and X.209. It notes that X.690 requires encoded SET OF components to be sorted in ascending order under DER, but applications should not rely on the ordering of attribute components. References to PKCS #6 were removed because RSA Laboratories was withdrawing support for it. The number 1.7 avoids confusion with RFC 2314 (called version 1.5) and an unsupported version 1.6.

The security considerations section is a single sentence: security issues are discussed throughout the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: This edition tidies the old form, points to the newest rule books, and skips a feature that was being retired.
